name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,359

entries.clue: Company probing popular hero (4)

indicatorNotes.probing: to probe a thing is to push into it, so the piece doing the probing ends up inside the other

blocks.note: in = popular, as in the in crowd
co. = company, the abbreviation on a letterhead

annotation.surface: A firm is looking into a well-liked public figure.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the single word at the end, where the surface wants it to be the thing under investigation. CO for company and IN for popular are two of the shortest pieces a setter has.
annotation.definitionFit: An icon is a figure held up for admiration, which is 'hero' in the sense of someone looked up to rather than someone brave.

entries.clue: Extinct creature is around, somehow (8)

indicatorNotes.somehow: 'somehow' says the thing came about by means unexplained, and letters that arrived by unexplained means are letters out of their given order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: Something long dead is said to be somewhere nearby.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Around' looks like a position word and 'is' like ordinary grammar, so neither reads as material. The comma before the indicator is the only hint that the sentence has stopped describing and started instructing.
annotation.definitionFit: Dinosaurs are the creatures everyone reaches for when asked to name something extinct, so the definition works by example rather than synonym.

entries.clue: Former manager protects somewhat fishy character (6)

indicatorNotes.protects: whatever protects something keeps it inside itself, so these words are sheltering the answer within them
indicatorNotes.somewhat: 'somewhat' means only part of what is written is wanted, not the whole of it

blocks.note: forMER MANager conceals the answer across the join between the two words

annotation.surface: An ex-boss is shielding a slightly shady individual.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fishy' is the pivot: the surface wants it for shifty, and the definition means it literally, from the waist down. The hidden run straddles two words, which is why it survives a quick read.
annotation.definitionFit: A merman is the male counterpart of a mermaid, half man and half fish, so 'fishy character' describes him plainly rather than accusing him of anything.

entries.clue: Calm dates sadly unknown (6)

indicatorNotes.sadly: 'sadly' concedes that something has not turned out as it should, and letters that have not turned out as they should are letters to rearrange

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters
y is the algebraist's unknown quantity, joined to the fodder

annotation.surface: Nobody has managed to pin down when the quiet days fall.
annotation.walkthrough: X, Y and Z all stand for an unknown in crosswords, borrowed from school algebra, and Y is the one that turns up most. 'Calm' is an adjective here, matching the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone steady is calm and unflustered, the sense of 'steady nerves' rather than the sense of unchanging speed.

entries.clue: Nicked criminal lets on (6)

indicatorNotes.criminal: calling something criminal says it is not as it ought to be, and letters not as they ought to be want reordering

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters

annotation.surface: A crook is letting slip rather more than he intended.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nicked' is British slang for both stolen and arrested, and it is the arrest sense that makes 'criminal' sit so comfortably beside it. 'Lets on' means reveals, and here supplies only letters.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Nicked' is British slang for taken without permission, and like the answer it is a past participle, so the swap is direct.

entries.clue: Flat happening to be incomplete (4)

indicatorNotes.incomplete: what is incomplete stops before it should, so the word is taken without its final letter

blocks.note: the noun sense — a happening is an occurrence — with the last letter T taken off

annotation.surface: A project that is under way has not been finished.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flat' means level, not an apartment or a punctured tyre. 'Happening to be' reads as idle filler, and a solver skims past it looking for the wordplay somewhere else.
annotation.definitionFit: An even surface is flat — level and free of bumps — which is the adjective the definition offers rather than the noun.

entries.clue: Person with positive intentions or odd ego, possibly (2,6)

indicatorNotes.possibly: 'possibly' leaves matters open rather than settled, so the letters before it are free to fall in another order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: Someone who means well, or else just has a strange opinion of himself.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Odd' is the trap: it normally asks for alternate letters, and here it only describes an ego. The definition runs to four words, which is why the fodder is so hard to see as fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A do-gooder acts from positive intentions, though the word carries a sneer at the meddling that the neutral definition leaves out.

entries.clue: How one talks about eg passport mishap (8)

indicatorNotes.about: to put one thing about another is to wrap it round, so the first piece closes over the second

blocks.note: the way a person talks is their accent
a passport is one example of ID

annotation.surface: Someone's way of speaking comes up in the story of a passport going wrong.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Eg' is the signal: it marks the passport as an example of something broader, so the letters wanted are the category and not the document. The definition is the last word, where the surface wants it to belong to 'passport'.
annotation.definitionFit: An accident is a mishap — an unplanned thing going wrong — and both are neutral nouns for the same event.

entries.clue: One Direction’s opener extremely grave and tense (2,4)

indicatorNotes.opener: the opener is whatever comes first, so the word is asked for its opening letter only
indicatorNotes.extremely: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so the letters wanted are the outermost ones

blocks.note: the word as it stands
the opening letter of DIRECTION
the extremes of GRAVE, its first and last letters

annotation.surface: One Direction's debut single was an extremely solemn record.
annotation.walkthrough: One Direction are a British boy band, and the band name is what stops you reading 'One' as a number sitting beside a compass word. The definition is the last word alone.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone on edge is tense — jumpy, unable to settle — and the phrase does the same adjective's work as the definition.

entries.clue: Casual school group following in a line (8)

indicatorNotes.following: what follows comes after, so the school group takes its place behind the word it is following

blocks.note: the word as it stands
a form is a year group in a British school — the fourth form, and so on
the word as it stands
l = line, the standard abbreviation

annotation.surface: A class is falling in behind someone in a queue.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Following' is the whole difficulty: it sends the school group after a word printed before it, so the answer runs against the order the sentence reads. FORM for a class is British schoolroom vocabulary.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal means casual — relaxed in manner or dress — and the two adjectives swap straight over.

entries.clue: A short former name for Thailand’s continent (4)

indicatorNotes.short: a word cut short is a word handed over without its last letter

blocks.note: the word as it stands
Thailand was called Siam until 1939, and SIAM cut short leaves SIA

annotation.surface: A quick note on what Thailand used to be called and where it sits.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is standing for 'is' and merely joining the halves, not marking a possessive, which is why Thailand belongs to the wordplay and the continent to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Asia is one of the continents, so the definition names the answer by its class rather than by a synonym.

entries.clue: Better lake in North America (8)

blocks.note: ranked above, the comparative sense
the northernmost of the Great Lakes, on the Canada–United States border

annotation.surface: One of the North American lakes is being rated the better one.
annotation.walkthrough: Two definitions with no letters moved at all, and the join is invisible because 'better' reads as an adjective describing the lake. Superior is the largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area.
annotation.definitionFit: Superior means better, ranked above; and Superior is also the name of a Great Lake, so the second half is a proper noun rather than a synonym.

entries.clue: Japan intend only to retain one of their video game companies (8)

annotation.definition: one of their video game companies

indicatorNotes.to retain: to retain something is to keep hold of it inside, so these words are holding the answer within them

blocks.note: japaN INTEND Only hides the answer across three words

annotation.surface: Japan means to keep just one of its games firms.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Their' points back at Japan, so the same word names the country in the definition and starts the hidden run in the wordplay. Eight letters spanning three words is a long hide, which is what makes it sit so quietly.
annotation.definitionFit: Nintendo is a Japanese video game company, so the definition picks the answer out by example from a group the clue has already named.

entries.clue: Anger is rather evident at first (3)

indicatorNotes.at first: 'at first' points to where each word starts, so only the opening letters are taken

blocks.note: the opening letter of IS
the opening letter of RATHER
the opening letter of EVIDENT

annotation.surface: Someone's temper shows itself early on.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the first word rather than the last, and the three initials run through a phrase that reads as a plain remark about a rising temper.
annotation.definitionFit: Ire is anger — a formal, slightly literary noun for it, and a noun is what the definition offers.

entries.clue: No longer quoting? That’s far from dull (8)

blocks.note: ex- means former, no longer holding the role
to cite something is to quote it

annotation.surface: Someone has stopped quoting other people, and that is welcome news.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: an ex-citer is not a thing anybody has ever been, and the answer only sounds as though it were. EX for former is among the first pieces a solver learns.
annotation.definitionFit: Something exciting is the opposite of dull, and 'far from dull' places it at the far end of that scale rather than merely off it.

entries.clue: Who can sign a very quiet Blackburn player? (8)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is put as a question rather than a noun: the answer is the person who answers it, and the question mark is the setter's licence for that.

blocks.note: the word as it stands
pp is pianissimo, the mark for 'very quiet' on a musical score
Blackburn Rovers are an English football club, so one of their players is a Rover

annotation.surface: Who is allowed to sign a rather subdued Blackburn Rovers footballer?
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sign' is transfer-market language in the surface and paperwork in the definition, and that double life is what holds the two halves of the clue together. PP comes from sheet music.
annotation.definitionFit: An approver is the person whose signature authorises a thing, so the definition names them by the act that defines them.

entries.clue: Empty tin in larger vessel (6)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' puts the piece named before it inside the piece named after it

blocks.note: a vat is a large vessel, comfortably bigger than a tin
a tin is a can

annotation.surface: An empty tin has been left standing inside a bigger container.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Larger' is comparing the two vessels, and the comparison is honest: a can really would fit in a vat. 'Empty' is the definition and means unoccupied rather than emptied out.
annotation.definitionFit: A vacant seat or room is empty — nobody in it — which is the adjective rather than the verb 'empty'.

entries.clue: For example, I’m entering concerning administration (6)

indicatorNotes.entering: what enters goes inside, so the pieces named before it are set within the piece named after

blocks.note: re = concerning, as at the head of a memo
e.g. = for example
the letters of I'm, taken as written

annotation.surface: I am joining an administration, for instance.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma after 'For example' makes it read as a throwaway aside, so it slips by as punctuation instead of as two letters. RE for concerning is the memo abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: A regime is an administration — the set of people running a country — with an extra flavour of being an unloved one that 'administration' leaves out.

entries.clue: Irish city seal (4)

blocks.note: the city on the river Lee in the south of Ireland
the stopper pushed into a bottle neck

annotation.surface: The official seal of a city in Ireland.
annotation.walkthrough: Three words are all the setter needs, because both readings are already lying there. The capital letter on Cork is the only thing the surface has to hide, and starting the clue hides it.
annotation.definitionFit: Cork is Ireland's second city; and a cork is what seals a bottle, so the same four letters answer to a place and to a stopper.

entries.clue: Suspend change internally (4)

indicatorNotes.internally: internally means on the inside, so the outside letters are left where they are and only the inside is taken

blocks.note: cHANGe without its outer letters

annotation.surface: An organisation is putting off a reshuffle of its own staff.
annotation.walkthrough: The hiding place is one short word, which is much harder to spot than a run across several. 'Suspend' means hang up rather than postpone, though the surface is content with either.
annotation.definitionFit: To hang something is to suspend it, leaving it dangling from a fixed point above.

entries.clue: Ponder? Ace got it sorted (8)

indicatorNotes.sorted: to sort things is to put them into a new order, which is what these letters are waiting for

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: A star performer got the whole problem straightened out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sorted' is British for dealt with, so the surface reads as praise rather than as an instruction. The question mark after the first word is the warning that the definition stops there.
annotation.definitionFit: To cogitate is to ponder — to turn a matter over in the mind — and both are verbs in the same plain form.

entries.clue: Double to Wizard of Oz character (4)

indicatorNotes.Double: to double a thing is to write it twice over, so the word that follows is used two times

blocks.note: the word as it stands
the same word again, because it was asked for twice

annotation.walkthrough: Toto is Dorothy's little dog in The Wizard of Oz, the one who pulls back the curtain at the end. The italics mark the title, which is the clue's only signal that a name is wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: Toto is Dorothy's dog in The Wizard of Oz, so the definition picks him out as one of that story's cast.

entries.clue: Some dip in a tasteful container of sweets (6)

indicatorNotes.Some: 'Some' asks for a part and not the whole, and the part wanted runs unbroken through the words that follow

blocks.note: diP IN A TAsteful hides the answer across four words

annotation.surface: There is some dip sitting in an elegant bowl of sweets.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like the containment instruction such clues usually carry, and it is only more fodder. A piñata is the Mexican party figure children break open for the sweets packed inside it.
annotation.definitionFit: A piñata is filled with sweets and hung up to be beaten open, so 'container of sweets' says what it is for rather than what it looks like.

entries.clue: Suggest an item on bananas (8)

indicatorNotes.bananas: to go bananas is to go mad, and letters sent mad will not stay in the order they were given

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: There is an item about bananas on the agenda.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On' belongs to the fodder rather than joining the halves, and seeing that is what makes the letter count come right. 'Bananas' for mad hides as the subject the meeting is discussing.
annotation.definitionFit: To nominate someone is to suggest them for a post or a prize, so the two verbs swap straight over.

entries.clue: Shining light originally replaced by British Rail (6)

indicatorNotes.originally: what a word is originally is how it begins, so the letter marked out is the one at the front
indicatorNotes.replaced by: 'replaced by' takes one piece out and puts the next piece into the gap it leaves

blocks.note: what a word is originally is the letter it opens with, and that is the piece which makes way
British Rail was the state-owned company that ran Britain's trains until it was broken up in the 1990s
the tail of the word, which survives the swap untouched

annotation.surface: The lamp that was there first has been swapped out by the railway.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Replaced by' reads as an ordinary verb in a maintenance report, and that is the disguise: it is really the instruction. The nationalised railway is long gone, but its initials are still crossword currency.
annotation.definitionFit: Bright means shining — giving off strong light — and both work as adjectives for a lamp or a morning.
